text: Most tables have a few columns that should fill in automatically most of the time — a created-at timestamp, an active flag that starts true. DEFAULT constraints handle exactly that, without you having to supply a value on every single insert.

CreatedAt datetime2 not null default, sysdatetime open paren close paren. IsActive bit not null default, 1. Omit both columns from the insert and SQL Server fills them in automatically — the current timestamp, and the value 1.

Here's the detail that trips people up: a default only kicks in when the column is left out of the insert's column list entirely. Write an explicit null for that column instead, and SQL Server inserts null — it does not fall back to the default.

Alter table dbo dot LessonDemo2, add constraint DF underscore LessonDemo2 underscore Status, default 'Pending' for Status. Just like primary keys, you can name a default constraint explicitly, giving you something predictable to reference later if you need to drop or change it.
Next lesson: computed columns — a column whose value is calculated from other columns in the same row, not stored by default.
